title: The Office of People Who Have Something to Tell You
subtitle: Character stories, dialogue and consequential choices

opening.title: The Listening Fee Nobody Agreed To
paragraphs: I opened the Office of People Who Have Something to Tell You with a gold microphone, six upholstered chairs, and a sign that said I UNDERSTAND. The sign cost more than the chairs. That was deliberate. A chair supports one person. My understanding was intended to support an entire market.

Shawna arrived carrying the enormous game binder against her hip. The spine had developed the soft, defeated curve of a man asked to attend another meeting. She set it on the table. One chair rose half an inch. Tank caught the coffee before my administration could baptize its own documents.
“Why is there a microphone?” Shawna asked.
“So nobody feels unheard.”
She touched the switch. My voice came out of a speaker in the bathroom.
“They hear you flushing,” Tank said.

I explained that this was a pilot arrangement. Mercedes explained that every arrangement I did not understand was apparently a pilot, and that I should stop allowing aircraft into the furniture budget. Rosa unplugged the speaker. Instantly the room became capable of conversation.

The proposal was simple. People in these games had jobs, friends, secrets, ambitions, terrible employers, and requests that did not fit into a yes-or-no box. We would listen. We would notice whose company felt interesting. We would find a story worth sitting inside. I had expanded that proposal into a department with a Director of Emotional Weather because a title that good should not have to wait for an actual vacancy.
Rosa read the first sheet. “You have charged a handling fee for feelings.”
“Fictional fee.”
“It has your bank details.”
“Fictional ambition.”

She drew one line through the amount and another through the account number. I admired her commitment to clarity even as she dismantled my retirement. Then she placed a bowl of oranges where the invoice tray had been. Everybody understood the new system immediately. You took an orange. You could talk. You could also remain completely quiet, an option my draft had neglected to monetize.
Mercedes sat in the chair facing the window. “Some of these stories are sad.”
“We have tissues.”
“That isn't a recommendation.”

She was right. A box of tissues did not make every story the right company for every evening. A game about grief might be welcome because it took grief seriously. On another evening the same game might feel like somebody delivering a piano through your chest. The reader got to decide. My stamp, though gold and offensively heavy, could not settle the matter.
Tank opened the binder at a page covered in resource bars. “This one wants me to manage food.”
“Narrative food.”
“I'm already managing real food. Rosa got the last orange.”

Here was the second distinction I had tried to bury beneath stationery: a game could wait for a decision and still make that decision feel pressured. A calendar, a dwindling supply, a political bargain, a friendship with consequences—none required quick fingers to produce a tight stomach. We needed to say what the demands actually were. We also needed to let a perfectly good game remain a perfectly good game that somebody did not want tonight.
Shawna moved my microphone to the end of the table. “And a lot of reading is still a lot of reading.”
I put that on the board. Under it I wrote NO EXAM AFTERWARD. Tank added UNLESS AIDEN HAS LOST HIS KEYS AGAIN. The keys were in my pocket. I made a point of finding them silently.

The reader's chair was not at the end of the table beneath the seal. Rosa put it wherever the reader wanted. Mercedes turned the screen so other people could follow without leaning across whoever held the controls. We agreed that a shared story did not automatically become a multiplayer game. Sometimes one person clicked while the others offered theories. Sometimes everybody shut up so a line could land. Sometimes the best contribution was bringing water and not explaining the joke.
I tried the microphone again. Nothing happened. I checked the cord, the switch, the speaker, and the magnificent little green light. Shawna watched me conduct a full technical inquiry.
“It's unplugged,” she said.
“I know.”
“Then why keep talking into it?”
Because, privately, I had been hoping my position would supply electricity.
We opened the first page without amplification. The tiny red stapler rested beside the oranges. For once it was not holding together a policy. It was keeping the window from knocking shut.

games.title: Coffee Talk
games.case_title: The Espresso Machine Requests a Confidentiality Agreement
scene: I installed a velvet rope around the coffee machine because the first game concerned intimate conversations, and intimacy deserved a premium entrance. Tank walked around the rope to reach the sugar. That exposed a structural weakness in my business model.
“You're supposed to tell me your problem first,” I said. “Then I prepare the appropriate drink.”
“My problem is a rope in front of the sugar.”

Shawna watched me remove it. On the screen, Coffee Talk offered a counter in an alternate Seattle where fantasy people had recognizable troubles. I immediately proposed separate departments for elves, orcs, and people who ordered something complicated. Rosa replaced all three signs with CUSTOMERS.

I brewed a cup of real coffee and began explaining how its bitterness represented the customer's journey. Mercedes tasted it. “It represents you forgetting the water.” She made another pot while I listened to a fictional conversation that managed, without a velvet rope, to be interesting. The office's first successful intervention was letting somebody else use the kitchen.
games.pleasure: Coffee Talk makes a café counter into a place to get to know recurring people. The fantasy setting puts a fresh surface on work, romance, identity, and belonging. Serving drinks influences story branches; the appeal is noticing a person's request and watching relationships develop.
games.burden: Use the main story with manual text advance; avoid timed Challenge mode. Expect substantial reading and ingredient selection. Drink choices can change story branches. Check the brewing interface and text controls; any decorative latte work is a separate hold/drag question.
games.first: Choose the main Story mode and manual text advance. Serve one early request, then stay for the conversation it supports. Notice whether ingredients add pleasure or interrupt listening; check the exact edition’s controls before settling in.
games.ruling: Admitted because the guests have interesting lives and my coffee machine has finally been demoted from therapist to appliance.

games.title: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly
games.case_title: The Second Cup Has Retained Counsel
scene: When the café returned with hibiscus and butterfly pea, I announced a botanical expansion of the listening office. I put a fern behind reception. It had no duties, but its posture suggested excellent discretion.
“That's plastic,” Rosa said.
“Then it won't repeat anything.”
Tank arrived with two cups bearing identical elaborate swirls. I praised his mastery of latte art. He turned one over. It was a saucer. The artistic department had been operating at an angle.

The sequel's customers already had lives before I entered the room. That offended my instinct to introduce everybody, but Mercedes insisted that catching up was a pleasure of returning. Shawna found me preparing an official welcome speech for a fictional barista who had done the job before.

She crossed out the speech and wrote LISTEN FIRST. I drew a heart in the margin. It looked like a dented radish. The plastic fern declined to comment, maintaining the strongest professional record of anybody I had hired that day.
games.pleasure: The second Coffee Talk offers more café conversations with returning and new fantasy customers, additional drink ingredients, and latte-art play. It suits an appetite for spending more time with this particular world rather than racing through a chain of dramatic reveals.
games.burden: Recipes and returning relationships can increase the things to remember. The official description includes fluid-simulation latte art, so drawing or held-pointer demands need checking separately. Nothing about the calm presentation establishes a complete absence of fiddly inputs.
games.first: Make an early drink and follow one customer's situation. Try the art interface only if it interests you; inspect how to proceed if it does not. Decide whether the return feels welcoming or depends too much on previous familiarity.
games.ruling: Approved for an evening when catching up with fictional regulars sounds better than hearing my new employee-orientation speech.

games.title: VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action
games.case_title: The Bartender Refuses My Corporate Mission Statement
scene: I put on a silver jacket to demonstrate cyberpunk readiness. The jacket reflected the lamp into Tank's eyes. He rotated my chair until I faced the wall, which apparently solved both the lighting problem and the presentation.
“I'm building atmosphere,” I said.
“You're building a second sun.”

In VA-11 Hall-A, the bar's customers carried news of a corporate dystopia into conversations about ordinary life. I designed a cocktail called The Synergy. It contained five ingredients and no clear purpose. Mercedes asked whether it came with a mandatory team-building exercise.

Shawna took over the measuring while I tried to remember whose drink required what. It was a useful correction: running a fictional bar involved an interface and requests, not just leaning against a counter looking expensive. Rosa gave my jacket to the back of a chair. The chair immediately looked more employable. I stopped inventing drinks long enough to discover that the people ordering them were the interesting part.
games.pleasure: The game uses bartending to frame a series of conversations about life in a high-tech, unequal city. Drinks influence which stories unfold. Its attraction is the contrast between large political systems and the specific people living, working, joking, and struggling inside them.
games.burden: Reading, recipe selection, and remembering customer preferences are real parts of the experience. Sexual conversation, alcohol, and adult subject matter belong to its tone. Check ingredient operations and any mixing or waiting controls rather than inferring simplicity from the visual-novel label.
games.first: Complete one customer order with the recipe information available on screen. Then judge the conversation itself: are these people enjoyable company, and is the bar routine a satisfying rhythm rather than unwanted clerical work?
games.ruling: Licensed to serve intrigue, provided nobody mistakes my metallic jacket for a required peripheral or a source of useful illumination.

games.title: The Red Strings Club
games.case_title: The Pottery Wheel Knows Too Much
scene: I welcomed the pottery wheel as evidence that corporate espionage had finally developed a respectable arts budget. Tank asked whether I knew how to use it. I assured him that my hands understood luxury.
The clay collapsed immediately.
“Your hands have issued a correction,” Shawna said.

The Red Strings Club combines conversations with bartending, shaping implants, and impersonating voices. I had assumed a game about talking would permit me to delegate all physical technique to my charisma. The little ruined bowl in front of me suggested otherwise.
Mercedes examined my attempt. “What is it?”
“A vessel for difficult questions.”
“It has no bottom.”

Rosa set a plate beneath it. We discussed whether happiness imposed by a corporation sounded like a service or a threat, while my vessel leaked onto a napkin. For once my failure had produced a relevant metaphor. I attempted to claim that this had been intentional. The entire room declined, politely but with excellent coordination.
games.pleasure: This cyberpunk conspiracy story asks what happiness and emotional freedom mean. Its unusual sequence of bartending, implant pottery, and phone impersonation gives those arguments different forms; you manipulate both objects and conversations while learning what a corporation intends.
games.burden: The store explicitly describes a lathe and cocktail manipulation, which makes pointer precision and held movement significant checks. This is not safely described as dialogue-only. Its emotional manipulation and corporate-control themes may also feel sharper than a relaxed conversation game.
games.first: Inspect the first hands-on task as soon as it appears. Determine whether its movement is enjoyable and whether the offered controls work for you. A compelling ethical question is not an obligation to tolerate an irritating interface.
games.ruling: Provisionally admitted because my bottomless bowl has demonstrated why every philosophy department needs a practical spill tray.

games.title: Neo Cab
games.case_title: Five Stars for Not Explaining the City
scene: I appointed myself the office's mobility visionary and sat in a parked car wearing driving gloves. Shawna held the keys outside my window. Apparently the position did not include access to the fleet.

Neo Cab's Lina makes a living transporting people through an automated city while searching for a missing friend. I prepared a passenger questionnaire with a section called OPINIONS ABOUT YOUR EXCEPTIONAL DRIVER. Mercedes used it to shade her eyes.
“What does the passenger want?” she asked.
“Transportation.”
“Try starting there.”
Tank got in and requested the kitchen. I delivered an unnecessary speech about the future of cities. He got out, walked six steps, and arrived before my conclusion. Rosa awarded him five stars.

The game put conversations, income, and emotional state into the same working life. That was more interesting than my imaginary steering credentials. I took off the gloves and read the next exchange. Shawna left the keys where they were.
games.pleasure: Neo Cab is a visual novel about Lina, a human driver in an increasingly automated city. Passengers become sources of stories and possible leads in her search. Her emotional state affects available responses, giving conversations a connection to the strain of working and surviving.
games.burden: Do not confuse its driving premise with a promise about vehicle controls: the inspected listing calls it a visual novel and declares a mouse-only option. Money, ratings, and emotion restrictions can still create pressure. Check reading flow and map/menu operations.
games.first: Follow an early passenger conversation through to its outcome. Look at how a mood change affects the next available response. Decide whether that constraint deepens the character or makes the conversation feel less enjoyable.
games.ruling: Receives a route permit because the passengers have more to say than my glove-based transportation strategy.

games.title: Eliza
games.case_title: The Microphone Has Been Replaced by a Script
scene: I hired myself as the human face of an automated listening service. The face was excellent. The service consisted of Shawna passing me cards from behind a screen.
“Please describe the issue,” I read.
Tank pointed at the screen. “You're behind a curtain in the dining room.”

The next card said ACKNOWLEDGE CONCERN. I acknowledged it in a voice I believed sounded professionally upholstered. Mercedes pulled the curtain aside. There was Shawna, the cards, and my invoice printer. The entire technological revolution fit on a folding table.

Eliza asks what happens when a human worker delivers words supplied by a counseling system. Rosa made clear that our game discussion was about a fictional workplace and its questions, not a service anybody here was receiving. I nodded and put the cards down.
Without the script, I had to decide what I actually thought. It took longer. The answer was less polished. For the first time that afternoon, it also belonged to me.
games.pleasure: Eliza follows Evelyn as she works as a human proxy for an AI counseling program and reconnects with people from her past. Fully voiced characters and a contemporary setting carry questions about work, responsibility, technical power, and whether simulated care meets real needs.
games.burden: The subject includes personal distress and the limits of counseling technology. Consider whether that is welcome material tonight. Expect substantial dialogue and choices; verify text pacing and navigation. This is a fictional story, not an instruction manual for supporting another person.
games.first: Read an early work scene and a conversation outside it. Compare the constrained professional role with Evelyn's own voice. Continue if the contrast makes you curious, rather than because the subject seems worthy enough to require homework.
games.ruling: Granted a hearing after my automated empathy platform was revealed to be Shawna with index cards and better judgment.

games.title: Citizen Sleeper
games.case_title: The Dice Have Unionized
scene: I rolled six dice across the table to allocate the afternoon's work. Every result assigned the unpleasant tasks to Tank. He inspected the sheet, then the dice, then me.
“Why does every number mean Tank?”
“Elegant interface.”

Shawna rewrote the allocation table while Rosa moved the snacks out of the resource pool. In Citizen Sleeper, dice and cycles shape the life of someone escaping corporate ownership on a space station. I found its distinction between available actions and endless demands uncomfortably relevant to my staffing policy.
Mercedes gave me one die and the printer manual. “Use your opportunity.”
The page I needed was underneath the binder. I spent my turn moving it. Tank spent his making tea. His choice immediately improved the station.

The game would wait for an input; that did not make its scarcity disappear. We could think carefully and still feel the pull between a useful job and a person worth helping. My dice system had finally encountered a consequence it could not assign elsewhere.
games.pleasure: Citizen Sleeper turns life on a crowded station into choices about work, friendships, resources, and survival. Assigning dice creates a clear connection between what you can do this cycle and what you care about. Its characters make those allocations feel personal rather than merely numerical.
games.burden: Steam declares playable without timed input, but the story uses resource pressure and advancing clocks. Several systems and ongoing relationships need attention. That declaration does not verify hold-free controls; inspect dice placement, text size, and the station interface.
games.first: Spend one cycle slowly, explaining to yourself what each chosen action will cost or advance. Meet somebody whose situation interests you. Notice whether the limited opportunities feel engaging or like a second schedule to manage.
games.ruling: Approved when you want meaningful tradeoffs and can tolerate the dice refusing to fund my entire executive department.

games.title: Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector
games.case_title: The Escape Ship Has a Procurement Committee
scene: I unveiled our escape ship using a cardboard box, a kitchen timer, and three chairs. Tank asked what we were escaping. I gestured toward the commission's paperwork.
“You made the paperwork.”
“Then I understand the threat.”

Citizen Sleeper 2 moves between habitats with a ship, crew, and risky contracts. I appointed Mercedes navigator without asking whether she wanted the role. She navigated directly out of my cardboard vessel. Rosa followed with the snacks. The crew's first joint decision was excellent.

Shawna stayed long enough to examine my maintenance budget. I had spent most of it on a gold captain's plate. She set it beneath a wobbling chair, turning decorative authority into a functioning repair.

Contracts in the game would require preparation and decisions about stress and resources. My fictional command had already illustrated why choosing companions involved more than collecting names. I asked the others whether they wanted to return. They did, on the condition that I stop referring to the living room as deep space.
games.pleasure: The sequel expands the dice-driven roleplaying into travel, crew-building, and contracts across an asteroid belt. A battered ship can become a home, while temporary jobs bring distinct characters and risks. The appeal is making a future through relationships as well as careful decisions.
games.burden: The current Steam record declares adjustable difficulty and play without timed input. It also describes stress, damaged dice, and multi-cycle contracts: waiting for you is not the same as removing consequences. Inspect the actual difficulty choices before relying on them.
games.first: Learn one contract's objective, available dice, and stress consequences before committing actions. Try a manageable early job and ask whether preparing with a crew adds pleasure or too many interconnected things to track.
games.ruling: Commissioned after the captain's nameplate proved better at supporting a chair than supporting my claim to leadership.

games.title: Disco Elysium - The Final Cut
games.case_title: My Necktie Has Requested a Separate Office
scene: I arrived in a spectacular tie and announced that the office required a detective. Tank asked what I had lost. I said that true investigation began before the crime. He checked whether I still had the receipt for the tie.

Disco Elysium filled a detective's head with competing perspectives. This struck me as efficient staffing. I already possessed confidence, ambition, and an inner voice insisting that expensive stationery would solve things. Shawna pointed out that none of them could locate the printer's power button.
Mercedes offered to voice my common sense. I objected that the role was already occupied. She waited. The silence established a vacancy.
Rosa studied the tie. “That thing's going to give advice, isn't it?”

In the game, the comedy and damage sit close together; a magnificent declaration can conceal a person in real trouble. I loosened my own tie before reading further. It had begun to feel like an unusually ornate argument I did not need to win.
games.pleasure: The Final Cut presents a dense, voiced detective roleplaying story about a damaged investigator and a politically complicated city. Skills become argumentative inner voices, making character-building part of the writing. Conversations can be funny, cruel, revealing, and unexpectedly tender.
games.burden: Expect extensive dialogue, skill checks, inventory and character menus, and mature material including addiction and violence. A failed choice can have consequences. The manually checked source confirms the Final Cut edition, but does not certify all interactions as untimed or hold-free.
games.first: Follow an early conversation and inspect one relevant skill explanation. Decide whether the competing voices delight you or interrupt the person you want to hear. Treat the opening as a test of tone as much as controls.
games.ruling: Admitted only after my tie's application for municipal funding was rejected on the grounds that it already consumed enough resources.

games.title: NORCO
games.case_title: The Refinery Declines My Mood Board
scene: I prepared a tasteful mood board for the industrial South. It contained a swamp photograph, a neon swatch, and a note reading ADD ATMOSPHERE. Mercedes looked at it for several seconds.
“Where are the people?”
I had left room in the lower corner, which did not improve my answer.

NORCO's world contains refineries, shops, family memories, strange technology, and people whose lives do not fit inside an aesthetic label. Shawna replaced my mood board with a map of who was missing and why the search mattered. Suddenly we had a reason to go somewhere.

Tank offered a stuffed monkey as our departmental mascot. I tried to give it a security clearance. Rosa took the badge away before I could pierce the fabric. The monkey's refusal to participate made it our most plausible investigator.

We followed the first thread of the story. My atmospheric swatches remained unused. Outside the window, a delivery truck backed up with an ugly practical beep. For once I let a place make its own sound.
games.pleasure: NORCO combines a missing-person search with family history, industrial landscapes, and increasingly strange science fiction in South Louisiana. Its dialogue-focused point-and-click structure invites attention to both particular characters and the forces shaping their world.
games.burden: The official description also mentions puzzles and fights; do not treat dialogue-focused as proof that every sequence is mechanically quiet. Expect dense imagery, unfamiliar connections, and bereavement. Check each new interaction type and the text/interface size.
games.first: Explore an early location and follow one clue about the missing brother. Pause to decide whether the place feels intriguing in its own right. Inspect the first unfamiliar mechanical sequence before assuming later play matches the opening.
games.ruling: Receives a travel warrant because an industrial landscape deserves more attention than my decorative label reading interesting decay.

games.title: Kentucky Route Zero
games.case_title: The Delivery Address Is Underneath the Road
scene: I took charge of route planning with a map so large that Tank had to stand outside the room to unfold it. Our destination was a secret highway beneath Kentucky. I drew a confident arrow through the middle of the table.
“That's not a road,” Shawna said.
“It's a conceptual route.”
“It's the sandwich grease.”

Kentucky Route Zero seemed less interested in rewarding my navigation credentials than in the people met along the way. A delivery, a debt, a conversation: ordinary things could open into rooms that felt like theater or a dream. Mercedes asked me to stop demanding that every strange image produce an immediate explanation.

I folded the map. It resisted. Tank folded me out of the way and dealt with it properly. Rosa left a small lamp on the table. We read the next scene without trying to turn it into a checklist. The grease mark remained where it was, giving our official route map its only reliable local landmark.
games.pleasure: This five-act magical-realist adventure follows a delivery into a world of strange roads, precarious work, debts, and fragile communities. Its pleasure lies in language, staging, music, and atmosphere. Choices can feel like shaping a performance rather than selecting the correct solution to a puzzle.
games.burden: Expect substantial reading, ambiguity, and a pace that may feel deliberately indirect. The PC Edition has been manually matched to the assigned complete game. Check movement and text advance; no inspected source establishes every scene as free of held or timed input.
games.first: Stay with one early encounter rather than trying to solve the whole world's meaning. Notice whether choosing a line makes you feel involved. If the theatrical distance leaves you cold, that is useful taste information, not a reading failure.
games.ruling: Granted an underground delivery permit because the address is interesting enough to survive my inability to fold its map.

games.title: Night in the Woods
games.case_title: The Reunion Committee Has Been Banned from the Roof
scene: I planned a homecoming party for myself even though I had only gone to the shop. Tank was instructed to say that I had changed. He said I had forgotten the milk.
“Emotionally changed.”
“Still no milk.”

Night in the Woods returns Mae to a town and friendships that have continued without her. I understood the desire to pick up an old role. I was less enthusiastic about the possibility that other people had developed their own opinions while I was away.
Mercedes took the welcome banner down from the doorway. “It has been nine minutes.”

Shawna pointed out that a story about hanging out could still ask us to move and jump through its town. I had been ready to approve it on the strength of autumn leaves alone. Rosa asked whether my leaf-based assessment included the roof I was now suggesting Tank climb to hang the banner. It did not. We left the banner at chair height and paid attention to the actual controls.
games.pleasure: Night in the Woods offers the company of young adults negotiating friendship, disappointment, work, and changes in their hometown. Its animal characters carry recognizably human conversations, with a mystery growing around the edges of daily wandering.
games.burden: Movement and platforming are part of its adventure structure, and additional activity types require checking. Do not file it as a static visual novel. Its themes can be bleak, including economic decline and emotional distress, despite the bright designs and frequent jokes.
games.first: Walk through an early stretch of town and talk to somebody who knows Mae. Test the movement before investing in the story. Decide whether the everyday conversations are reward enough for the amount of traversal between them.
games.ruling: Conditionally welcomed because a reunion should reveal how people changed, not just congratulate me for returning with the wrong groceries.

games.title: Beacon Pines
games.case_title: One Word Has Overturned the Entire Department
scene: I wrote a ceremonial sentence for the office: AIDEN WAS WISE. Mercedes replaced the last word with AVAILABLE. Tank replaced it with LATE. Rosa said both amendments could stand.

Beacon Pines makes words into objects that can alter a story's turning points. This was a dangerous precedent for a man who had invested heavily in controlling the minutes. I tried locking the marker in a drawer. Shawna opened it with the handle.
“Security needs work,” she said.

The book's inviting appearance did not mean every possible branch would be comforting. That interested Mercedes, who liked the friction between a charming surface and something wrong beneath it. I liked the possibility of revisiting a decision until somebody called me wise.

Tank collected the three word cards and arranged them into AIDEN WAS AVAILABLE LATE. It was both a correction and a workable office schedule. We let the fictional story keep its own surprises while my real sentence remained, at last, supported by evidence.
games.pleasure: Beacon Pines combines exploring a small town with collecting word charms and revisiting branches through a story tree. New words can transform a moment and open different events. Curiosity about how a sentence changes the world becomes part of solving its mystery.
games.burden: The Steam record declares play without timed input and keyboard-only operation. Branch tracking still adds a memory burden, and the cute art accompanies creepy events. Those declarations do not establish that every control avoids holds; test ordinary walking and menu selection.
games.first: Collect an early charm and use it at a turning point. Then inspect how the story tree represents the route. Continue if comparing possibilities feels like discovery rather than keeping several unfinished stories in your head.
games.ruling: Approved because the Department of One Carefully Chosen Word has achieved more reform than my complete annual report.

games.title: Mutazione
games.case_title: The Garden Has Heard About My Promotion
scene: I entered the community garden with a badge reading DIRECTOR OF GROWTH. Rosa asked which plant I had grown. I pointed at the plastic fern. She removed my badge without disturbing its leaves.

Mutazione's gardens and conversations offered a different kind of attention: visit, listen, learn how people were connected, and let a place become familiar. I began a gossip chart with myself in the center. Mercedes turned the paper over.
“You aren't in this town.”
“I could be a visiting dignitary.”
“You could be quiet for one conversation.”
Shawna listened to the musical garden while Tank arranged our actual plants so they could reach the window. One plant leaned away from my badge. I declined to interpret that as a performance review.

The story's community had secrets and pain as well as warmth. It did not need me to certify it wholesome. I sat down, asked Rosa what the real plant needed, and received the remarkably actionable answer: water, occasionally, without a speech.
games.pleasure: Mutazione follows Kai visiting her grandfather in an unusual island community. Conversations, old tensions, and musical gardens sit alongside the supernatural plot. Its attraction is spending enough time with a place that the relationships begin to matter.
games.burden: Illness, family secrets, and community conflict are central; gentle presentation is not a promise of emotionally light material. Steam declares no timed input, mouse-only and keyboard-only options, and save-anytime. Verify those options on the installed version and inspect ordinary navigation.
games.first: Meet one resident and spend time with an early garden interaction. Judge the balance between conversation and moving through the community. If you like it, a note of the next person to visit may make returning easier.
games.ruling: Admitted because the garden's useful advice was shorter than my title and considerably more likely to keep something alive.

games.title: Wytchwood
games.case_title: The Witch Has Rejected My Ingredient Spreadsheet
scene: I proposed a centralized inventory for the witch's cupboard. Everything received an impressive label. The first jar said PREMIUM BOTANICAL SOLUTION. Rosa opened it.
“Dried basil.”
“Branding.”

Wytchwood's old witch gathered peculiar materials and used them to intervene in other people's stories. I admired her confidence until Shawna pointed out that confidence did not collect the ingredients. Somebody still had to go find what the recipe required.

games.case_title: The Throne Has Run Out of Biscuits
scene: I built my throne from two office chairs, which gave it twice the authority and an alarming tendency to swivel in opposite directions. Petitioners were invited to approach with any problem that could be solved by a confident expression.

Tank needed a working kettle. Rosa needed the snack cupboard replenished. Mercedes requested that I stop calling the hallway my northern province. I granted all three requests verbally and then discovered that verbal grants do not heat water.

In Yes, Your Grace, a king must hear requests while his resources remain inconveniently finite. I regarded this as a terrible design flaw in monarchy. Shawna regarded it as the beginning of accounting.

She placed four coins beside six requests and watched me arrange them into a more optimistic shape. The coins remained four. Eventually I climbed down from the throne to help with the kettle. Both chairs immediately became more useful, which Tank said was my strongest policy result.
games.pleasure: King Eryk hears petitioners, manages scarce resources and tries to protect his family and kingdom. Small requests sit beside larger alliances and threats, giving decisions an immediate human face rather than reducing everything to an abstract national graph.
games.burden: Resources run out, requests conflict and family decisions can hurt. The presentation includes strategic preparation and dangerous events; a throne screen is not a promise of carefree play. Verify the controls and pause behavior in the chosen PC version before assuming all situations wait.
games.first: Hear the first petition and look at the resources attached to an answer. Ask whether saying no feels satisfyingly consequential or simply unpleasant. Stop without treating a difficult decision as something you must finish tonight.
games.ruling: Suitable when four coins and six requests sound like a story; unsuitable when you already chaired that meeting at breakfast.

games.case_title: Aiden's Search History Requests Legal Representation
scene: I demonstrated my new surveillance department by projecting my own browser history onto the office wall. It included searches for ceremonial cape storage, affordable marble that looks expensive, and whether a person can trademark the concept of arriving.
'Strong case,' Tank said.
I explained that these fragments had been cruelly separated from context. Shawna asked what context could possibly improve the marble query. I said architectural ambition. Mercedes said plastic.

Orwell made the exercise less comfortable. A digital trace can be true and still create the wrong picture when somebody chooses which piece to pass along. My department's excellent equipment consisted of a mouse, a projector and an alarming amount of confidence in itself.

Rosa switched off the projector before the cape measurements appeared. I thanked her for respecting due process. She said she was respecting everyone else's lunch. We agreed that access to a detail does not automatically make its use wise.
games.pleasure: You investigate digital records for a state surveillance program and decide what information to submit. The pleasure lies in connecting messages, profiles and apparent contradictions, then noticing how your selection shapes somebody else's fate.
games.burden: Expect substantial reading, interface switching and memory for names and relationships. Surveillance, terrorism and personal intrusion are central themes. Selecting or transferring evidence needs a direct input check; the premise alone cannot certify mouse-only ease, no dragging or an absence of timed sections.
games.first: Examine one person's available records and identify two details that might mean different things together. Before forwarding evidence, decide whether the ethical discomfort interests you. A companion can compare interpretations while one person operates the interface.
games.ruling: Approved for suspicious document readers, provided my search for a throne-sized lumbar cushion remains contextual evidence.

games.case_title: The Department of Technically Accurate Nonsense
scene: After my first surveillance scandal, I established a communications office. Its inaugural headline was AIDEN PROVIDES UNPRECEDENTED SEATING. Underneath sat a photograph of the chair I had finally returned to the kitchen.
'Every word is true,' I said.
'And somehow the sentence is still lying,' Shawna replied.

Orwell: Ignorance is Strength understands that territory: information gains power through its placement, selection and use. I tried writing a correction that celebrated my commitment to corrections. Mercedes crossed out everything except RETURNED A CHAIR.
Tank wanted to know why the public needed a statement about a chair at all. This was a devastating question for an institution with an entire stationery drawer devoted to statements.

Rosa moved the drawer out of the kitchen and asked us to set the table. For once, a useful event occurred without a headline. I privately described it as a successful pilot of our low-visibility domestic infrastructure initiative, but I had the decency to keep that inside my head.
games.pleasure: This second Orwell story places you in a darker investigation shaped by political narratives and information manipulation. It can reward a reader who enjoys noticing how an apparently factual detail becomes a persuasive weapon.
games.burden: The official description introduces a time-of-day system and decisions about whom to investigate and when. That establishes scheduling pressure inside the story, not a verified real-time countdown or a no-timer guarantee. Expect dense records, unsettling politics and morally compromised work.
games.first: Read the first assignment and inspect how the interface represents time before making several moves. Decide whether tracking opportunities sounds engaging. Discuss one competing interpretation with a companion without assuming the game offers a neutral choice.
games.ruling: For evenings when a misleading headline makes you want to inspect its footnotes; my chair announcement has been withdrawn.

games.case_title: My Away Message Is Longer Than My Visit
scene: I prepared for Emily is Away by constructing a nostalgic online persona. My screen name contained three titles, two mysterious numbers and enough punctuation to make it look like a damaged shipping address.
Tank chose Tank. This struck me as an irresponsible refusal to develop a brand.

My away message announced that I was pursuing destiny beyond the limits of ordinary communication. Rosa looked through the doorway and found me searching for a clean spoon. Mercedes suggested a more accurate status: available, but being weird about it.

The game's instant-message window made small choices feel exposed. A short answer can carry all the things somebody is unwilling or unable to say. I began composing a magnificent explanation of why my fictional younger self deserved universal understanding.
Shawna tapped the screen. 'You're supposed to hear the other person too.' I deleted three paragraphs. Somewhere in the abandoned punctuation, a much more plausible conversation began to breathe.
games.pleasure: A simulated desktop and instant messenger frame a relationship across several years. Buddy profiles, changing circumstances and brief exchanges turn a familiar piece of technology into a story about growing apart, uncertainty and what people leave unsaid.
games.burden: Reading is central, and the messenger presentation includes keyboard interaction that should be tried directly. Do not assume every message is simply a pointer click or that arbitrary typing works identically across versions. Relationship regret may carry more weight than the small interface suggests.
games.first: Choose a screen name and follow the first conversation far enough to feel its rhythm. Check the actual typing demand and text size. The useful question is whether the intimacy of messaging appeals, rather than whether you chose the best reply.
games.ruling: Recommended when an old away message can summon an entire era; my era apparently smelled of spoon polish and ambition.

games.case_title: The Campfire Refuses My Team-Building Exercise
scene: I announced a summer retreat for the office. Attendance was optional, although I had already embroidered everyone's names onto a banner reading TOGETHER WE VALIDATE AIDEN.
Mercedes inspected it. 'I opt out of the verb.'

We Know the Devil offered a much sharper picture of a group: three teenagers, a religious camp, and the way choosing closeness with one person can leave another outside. My icebreaker asked everybody to name a leadership quality they admired in me. The room became so silent that the printer's cooling fan sounded like weather.

Rosa took down the banner. Shawna replaced the exercise with a question anyone could decline to answer. Tank made a small campfire out of a battery lamp and some orange tissue paper, because he correctly distrusted my relationship with ceremonial flames.
I sat down without facilitating anything. Nobody applauded. The room improved anyway. It was an uncomfortable discovery for a man who had purchased a whistle specifically for fostering togetherness.
games.pleasure: This visual novel uses a small cast and a threatening camp setting to explore belonging, exclusion and queer identity. Which characters spend time together matters, creating room for conversation about relationships rather than inventory puzzles or navigation.
games.burden: Psychological horror, religious pressure, isolation and an alarming soundscape are integral to the experience. Light movement demands would not make the subject gentle. The inspected page supports its visual-novel form but does not independently verify every advance input or the absence of all timing demands.
games.first: Read the opening exchange and listen to a short portion of the atmosphere at a comfortable volume. Decide whether this kind of unease is welcome before pursuing a route. Nobody owes the camp a complete visit.
games.ruling: Admitted for people curious about an unsettling triangle of loyalties; my whistle is not permitted within camp boundaries.

games.case_title: The Missing Phone Contains Fourteen Pictures of My Elbow
scene: When somebody mentioned a found-phone mystery, I offered my own handset as a practice case. Its photographs consisted of my elbow, several meals I had forgotten to photograph until after eating them, and a blurry close-up of the gold stamp.
'We can establish one thing,' Shawna said. 'The suspect has never met a camera angle he understands.'

A Normal Lost Phone asks you to reconstruct a life from a fictional device. I started explaining that my contacts list revealed a complex network of influence. Tank showed us the entry for Kettle Guy, which was my own number from a failed repair appointment.

Rosa put the phone down. 'A real person's privacy isn't a party game.' The distinction held: this is a designed fictional investigation, with a story waiting behind its interface. My embarrassing photographs were merely an administrative failure. Mercedes deleted nothing, because evidence of my elbows deserved a fair hearing, however unflattering its composition.
games.pleasure: Messages, pictures and apps form a narrative investigation into Sam's life and disappearance. The appeal is close reading: an ordinary digital object gradually reveals relationships and circumstances that were invisible at first glance.
games.burden: The inspected Steam page says this game is no longer available on that store as of September 20, 2026. Existing access must be established before planning a session. Expect personal, potentially sensitive material, small interface details and searching across apps; the page does not certify input comfort.

games.ruling: Provisionally welcome for digital archaeologists; the committee must first locate the game, unlike my elbow, which is exceptionally well documented.

games.case_title: Laura's Calendar Declines an Interview with My Ego
scene: For the second phone investigation, I proposed an improved method: reconstruct somebody's life from their calendar. My own calendar contained Breakfast Strategy, Lunch Strategy and an unexplained three-hour appointment called Become Unignorable.
Mercedes said the last event appeared to be recurring.

Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story invites attention to the gaps between a person's public routine and private circumstances. I spread coloured cards across the table, certain that enough organisation would make another life simple.

Shawna separated what the records actually said from what I had guessed. Half my impressive diagram moved into the second pile. Tank added a third pile labelled AIDEN LIKES ARROWS. It was distressingly large.

Rosa asked what Laura might need us to notice, rather than what would make us feel clever. That question rearranged the whole table without a single new arrow. I cancelled Become Unignorable and scheduled Listen. Then I removed the alarm, since apparently listening was allowed to continue beyond its appointment.
games.pleasure: A fictional found phone holds Laura's photographs, messages and apps. Following connections between professional life, relationships and social habits creates a story through investigation rather than through moving an avatar around a large landscape.
games.burden: Expect close reading, app navigation, inference and difficult personal circumstances. games.case_title: A Narrator with a Very Suspicious Job Description
scene: I read the instruction aloud: go to the basement, deal with the princess, trust the narrator. This sounded wonderfully efficient to a man who routinely wrote his own glowing minutes.
Shawna asked why anyone should trust the narrator. I pointed at my official speaking jacket. Tank pointed at the fact that I had named it myself.

Slay the Princess made the dispute much less cosy. A voice can sound certain while the person listening has good reasons to question the assignment. I attempted to restore order with a sentence beginning Obviously. Mercedes stopped me before the second word.
Rosa said we could simply decline an evening of horror. This had not appeared anywhere in my dramatic briefing, because I had been busy choosing the basement font.

I rewrote the invitation. It now described the disturbing material and let people decide. The speaking jacket remained on its hanger, where its claims to moral authority could trouble only the spare umbrella and one exceptionally sceptical moth.
games.pleasure: The Pristine Cut expands a fully voiced psychological-horror visual novel whose branching story turns on what you do, believe and question. Narration, performance and shifting interpretations are major attractions for somebody who enjoys arguing with a story's apparent authority.
games.burden: The developer explicitly warns of intense violence, gore, partial nudity, strong language and suicide themes. This is a substantial content catch, not a gentle princess tale. Full voice acting does not establish no timed or held inputs; check the exact interface before making that assumption.
games.first: Read the content notice first. If the premise still appeals, hear the initial narration and inspect how dialogue advances. Choose whether to continue for its argument and atmosphere, without accepting the narrator's urgency as your own.
games.ruling: A conditional invitation for people who enjoy a sinister voice being challenged; my jacket failed the narrator-trust examination on sight.

games.case_title: The Family Reunion Has an Unscheduled Creature
scene: I arranged a perfectly normal family gathering on behalf of Scarlet Hollow. The seating chart accounted for old grievances, difficult conversations and one cousin who might bring an inexplicable object.
Tank asked why there was a place marked CRYPTID. I said good hospitality anticipated unusual guests. Rosa agreed about hospitality but asked why the cryptid had a better chair than everybody else.

The game combines a funeral visit, strained family ties and a town with deeply unwelcome mysteries. I selected personal traits for my fictional host, starting with Unmatched Charisma. Shawna asked whether a game actually offered that trait or whether I was filling in my own publicity again.

Mercedes chose a chair where she could see the door. I revised my seating chart to include a clear exit for anybody who disliked the horror. The cryptid never arrived, but my aunt's silence about the potato salad developed an atmosphere powerful enough to qualify for its own soundtrack.

interludes.title: The Committee for Leaving a Sentence Alone
paragraphs: By the middle of the afternoon, I had developed a method for responding to every fictional confession. I leaned forward, lowered my voice, and said, “That must be difficult.” It worked beautifully until Tank told me the printer was out of paper.
“That must be difficult,” I said.
“It must be loaded.”

Mercedes slid a sheet toward me. She had kept a record of my contributions. The same six words appeared seventeen times. At the bottom she had drawn my microphone inside a recycling bin. The drawing was very good. I considered commissioning a portrait before I understood the insult.
“Listening isn't waiting to deploy your sentence,” she said.

I wanted to object on professional grounds. Unfortunately the profession was one I had invented that morning, and its entire training consisted of buying the sign. Shawna took the page and folded it into a small stand for the screen. My empty reassurance was finally providing practical support.

We had reached the games where choices mattered in different ways. Some changed a line. Some spent a resource. Some opened or closed a route. Some simply let you express how a character regarded a thing that would happen anyway. None of these automatically made the others dishonest. The pleasure could be in steering events, in inhabiting a voice, or in noticing a detail that another person missed.

I proposed a universal significance scale. Rosa asked whether I could accurately scale the amount of tea left in my cup. I lifted it to demonstrate. It was empty. She refilled it without comment, which was both kind and a devastating audit.
Tank had found a conversation he wanted to finish. The rest of us were halfway through a discussion of what he should say. He raised one hand.
“Can I hear what they say first?”

We could. We did. The room became quieter than my expensive acoustic panels had ever managed to make it. A fictional person finished a thought. Tank chose a response none of us had suggested. It belonged to his reading of the scene, and nobody needed to win an argument about it.

That gave Shawna the policy she had wanted all day: suggestions by invitation. A companion could read aloud if asked. A companion could keep a note if wanted. A companion could solve a menu problem without taking over the character's life. If a difficult choice was part of the fun, we did not steal it in the name of being helpful.
I approved the policy with the gold stamp. The ink pad was dry.
“You can just say yes,” Rosa said.
I said yes. It left no embossed border, no seal, no glorious mark that future historians could place beneath glass. Everybody understood me anyway.
Outside the window, the wind changed. The red stapler held. My Director of Emotional Weather had produced less useful weather management than a stationery item with one visible screw.

ending.title: The Office Closes When the Guest Leaves
paragraphs: I had reserved the final hour for a grand address on the transformative power of narrative. The heading occupied half a page. Beneath it I had written REMEMBER TO BE HUMBLE in letters large enough to be read from the corridor.
Mercedes found it while looking for a clean sheet.
“You scheduled humility?”
“Otherwise it gets crowded out.”
“By what?”
I glanced at the microphone. She nodded as if that completed the paperwork.

Instead of the address, Rosa asked everybody what they actually wanted to return to. The answers were not a ranking. One person wanted another conversation at a counter. Another wanted a difficult political decision precisely because it was difficult. Somebody wanted a strange town. Somebody else had had enough reading and wanted dinner. Nobody had failed the afternoon by choosing dinner.

Tank named one character he liked and one menu he disliked. That was more useful than my twelve-column experience matrix. Shawna wrote the two observations on a small card. We could act on them. We could try a different game, make a short next-step note, or return another day. We did not need to invent a permanent identity for a person from one evening's taste.

I looked at the binder. Forty stories sat in this part of it, and each contained more lives, choices, and complications than any summary could comfortably hold. The book could point toward a door. It could tell you whether there appeared to be stairs behind it. It could admit when we had not inspected the stairs. It could not make you enjoy the room.
That was a smaller job than the one I had advertised. It was also an honest one.
Shawna began stacking the chairs. I stopped her after the second.
“Leave one.”
She waited.
“If somebody wants to keep going.”

We left the screen where it was, the water beside it, and the route note within reach. There was no ceremony of completion. A conversation could remain unfinished without becoming a debt. A game could be abandoned without insulting its creator. The office could still contain an open book after the person who opened it had decided to do something else.
Rosa handed me the sign. I UNDERSTAND still glittered across it in deeply unnecessary gold.
“What do you want to do with this?”
I turned it over. The back was plain white. With a marker, I wrote TELL ME MORE.
Mercedes studied it. “Better.”
Tank added OR DON'T beneath it.
That was the part that made it work.

We carried the oranges into the kitchen. I took the gold microphone with us because it turned out to be an excellent weight for holding down the corner of a curling recipe. My understanding finally had a practical assignment. It did not speak once.

The red stapler stayed at the window until the evening cooled. Then Shawna closed the window, picked it up, and put it beside the binder. Nothing was permanently fixed. Everything necessary remained within reach.
